artiest/anthony-kiedis.text:
Anthony Kiedis was born in 1962 in Grand Rapids, Michigan. After his parents divorced he grew up with his mother, but at the age of twelve he moved in with his father in Hollywood. At Fairfax High School in Los Angeles he became best friends with Flea, who introduced him to punk rock. Through Flea he met the guitarist Hillel Slovak.

The three took inspiration from Defunkt, a band that mixed punk and funk. With the drummer Jack Irons they played a single gig in 1983 under a long, funny name, performing one song on which Kiedis rapped about the music. Soon they were called Red Hot Chili Peppers. After the 1984 debut, the funk pioneer George Clinton produced the second album, Freaky Styley (1985). The years that followed were hard: Kiedis and Slovak became addicted to heroin, and Slovak died in 1988. The band carried on and became one of the biggest rock bands of the 1990s. Blood Sugar Sex Magik (1991) contains Give It Away and Under the Bridge.

Kiedis began as someone who whipped up the crowd and grew into a singer. His rhythmic, half-rapped vocals fitted Flea's slapping bass perfectly and made the Chili Peppers the model of funk rock. His lyrics were at first mostly about sex and life in Los Angeles; later they became more personal, about love, addiction and loss. Since 2000 he has said that he is clean. In 2012 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with the band.
artiest/anthony-kiedis.listen: Listen to Give It Away by Red Hot Chili Peppers. Notice how Anthony Kiedis spits out the words fast and rhythmically, more like a rapper than a singer, while Flea's bass leaps and slaps underneath.

artiest/anthony-newley.text:
Anthony Newley (24 September 1931 to 14 April 1999) was an English actor, director, comedian, singer and composer, born in Hackney, London. He left school at fourteen and worked as an errand boy for an advertising agency, but through a newspaper advertisement he ended up at the Italia Conti stage school. As a boy he appeared in Vice Versa in 1948 and played the Artful Dodger in David Lean's Oliver Twist. In the 1950s he made twenty-seven films for J. Arthur Rank. His breakthrough then came in the musical film Idol on Parade in 1959, in which he played a rock singer who has to do his military service.

From 1959 to 1962 he had twelve entries in the British charts, including two number ones. With his writing partner Leslie Bricusse he created the musical Stop the World – I Want to Get Off, which contains the song What Kind of Fool Am I?, winner of the Grammy for Song of the Year in 1963. Next came The Roar of the Greasepaint, the Smell of the Crowd, with Who Can I Turn To, and the songs for Doctor Dolittle. With Bricusse he received an Oscar nomination for Willie Wonka & the Chocolate Factory (1971), with Pure Imagination. With John Barry he wrote the title song of the Bond film Goldfinger. His television series The Strange World of Gurney Slade has cult status.

Newley was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 1989. He shows how a British pop singer of the early rock 'n' roll years grew into a performer of musicals and cabaret.
artiest/anthony-newley.listen: Listen to Pure Imagination, written by Newley and Bricusse, and notice the gentle melody and the dreamy lyrics. Can you hear how the song sounds like an invitation?

artiest/antoine-guerber.text:
Antoine Guerber is a French musician who directs the ensemble Diabolus in Musica. This ensemble for medieval music was founded in Paris in 1992 and is based in Tours. Guerber studied medieval music with Dominique Vellard at the Centre de Musique Médiévale in Paris and in the early music department of the Conservatoire National Supérieur in Lyon.

With his ensemble he made recordings covering a broad stretch of the Middle Ages. Examples are La Chambre des Dames from 1997, Missa Magna from 1999, with a Mass from the papal chapel at Avignon in the fourteenth century, and Carmina Gallica from 2002, with Latin songs from the twelfth century. Next came Honi soit qui mal y pense! with polyphonic music from the English royal chapels, Missa Se la face ay pale in 2004, La doce acordance with songs by trouvères in 2005, and Paris expers Paris, about the Notre-Dame school, 1170 to 1240, in 2006.

Guerber thus makes music that arose long before modern pop: sung songs of the trouvères, early polyphony and the Mass. His ensemble shows how alive this old music can sound when singers perform it with knowledge of the sources.
artiest/antoine-guerber.listen: Listen to a recording by Diabolus in Musica and notice the singing without orchestral or piano accompaniment. Try to hear how several voices follow one another.

artiest/anton-webern.text: Anton Webern studied musicology in Vienna and was one of Schoenberg's first pupils. He adopted the twelve-tone method and turned it into extremely concentrated music in which every note counts and silences weigh as heavily as sounds. His Symphony, Op. 21 of 1928 lasts only about ten minutes and is built from mirrorings and canons. After the Second World War he became the great example for the young serialists in Darmstadt.
artiest/anton-webern.listen: Listen to the first movement of the Symphony and hear how isolated notes leap from instrument to instrument, with plenty of silence in between.

artiest/antonia-maass.text:
Antonia Maass is a German singer who played a small but striking part in David Bowie's Berlin years. In 1977 Bowie recorded the album Heroes at Hansa Studio, close to the Berlin Wall, with Brian Eno and the producer Tony Visconti. Maass sang along as a backing vocalist in that period.

According to the well-known story, Bowie saw from the studio two lovers kissing by the Wall. They were Visconti and Maass. That scene became the image in the title song: two people who, just for a moment, are heroes by the Wall. Maass also helped with the German version of the song, Helden, in which Bowie sings part of the lyrics in German. On that version she is credited as a writer alongside Bowie and Eno. Helden was released as a single in West Germany in 1977.

In this way her name links one of the most famous rock songs of the 1970s with the divided city of Berlin. The song later became a symbol of longing for freedom on both sides of the Iron Curtain.
artiest/antonia-maass.listen: Listen to Helden, the German-English version of Heroes by David Bowie. Notice the moment when Bowie switches to German, and compare how the lyrics sound in that language and in English.

artiest/antonin-dvorak.text: Antonín Dvořák grew up in a Bohemian village and for years played the viola in the orchestra of the Prague theatre. Brahms helped him find a publisher, and his Slavonic Dances made him known throughout Europe. From 1892 to 1895 he directed a conservatory in New York, where he advised American composers to listen to spirituals and indigenous music. There he wrote his Ninth Symphony, Z nového světa (From the New World), with its famous Largo for cor anglais.
artiest/antonin-dvorak.listen: Listen to the Largo and hear how, after a series of solemn brass chords, the cor anglais plays a simple, homesick melody.

artiest/antonio-carlos-jobim.text: Antônio Carlos Jobim, nicknamed Tom, grew up in Rio de Janeiro and studied classical piano. He worked as an arranger for a record company and, with the poet Vinícius de Moraes, wrote songs for theatre and film. With João Gilberto he laid the foundations of bossa nova in 1958. He wrote songs such as Chega de Saudade, Desafinado, Corcovado, The Girl from Ipanema and Águas de Março, which became standards all over the world. His harmonies are rich and often chromatic, with influences from Debussy and Cool Jazz. In 1967 he played on an album with Frank Sinatra. In 1974 he made Elis & Tom with the singer Elis Regina.
artiest/antonio-carlos-jobim.listen: Hear how a simple melody keeps landing on a new, unexpected chord.

artiest/antonio-pappano.text:
Sir Antonio Pappano is a British-Italian conductor and pianist, born on 30 December 1959 in Epping, Essex. His family came from Castelfranco in Miscano in Italy, and his father was a singing teacher. When he was thirteen the family moved to Connecticut. After training in piano, composition and conducting he became a répétiteur at the New York City Opera at the age of twenty-one. Daniel Barenboim noticed his talent and made him an assistant at the Bayreuth Festival.

In 1990 Pappano became music director of the Norwegian Opera, and from 1992 to 2002 of the Théâtre Royal de la Monnaie in Brussels. From 2002 to 2024 he led the Royal Opera House at Covent Garden, longer than anyone before him. From 2005 to 2024 he was also in charge of the orchestra of the Accademia Nazionale di Santa Cecilia in Rome. Since 2024 he has been chief conductor of the London Symphony Orchestra. In 2023 he conducted the orchestra at the coronation of Charles III. His recordings include La bohème in 1996, La rondine in 1997, Il trittico in 1999 and Manon in 2000.

He received Gramophone Artist of the Year in 2000, was knighted in 2012 and in 2024 won the Olivier Award for opera once again. Pappano shows how a conductor, through his work with singers and a large orchestra, can keep the opera audience young and broad.
artiest/antonio-pappano.listen: Listen to a recording of La bohème under Pappano and notice how the orchestra follows the singers. Try to hear how the tempo moves with the emotion of the scene.

artiest/antonio-vivaldi.text: Antonio Vivaldi was a priest and violinist in Venice who for decades worked with the girls of the orphanage Ospedale della Pietà, whose orchestra drew visitors from all over Europe. He wrote hundreds of concertos and made the form fast, slow, fast the standard, with a recurring refrain for the whole orchestra. In Le quattro stagioni of 1725 soloist and orchestra depict birds, thunderstorms and ice, after poems that are printed in the score. Bach arranged several of his concertos.
artiest/antonio-vivaldi.listen: Listen to the beginning of La primavera and hear how the orchestra plays a cheerful refrain, after which three violins imitate the singing of birds.

artiest/antony-pitts.text:
Antony Pitts, born in 1969 in Farnborough, Kent, is an international composer, conductor and producer. His compositions are published by Faber Music, and CDs of choral music have appeared on Hyperion Records, along with recordings on Harmonia Mundi and Naxos, among others. In 1996 he won the Radio Academy's BT Award for Facing the Radio, an early interactive experiment on the internet. In 2004 he received the Prix Italia for A Pebble in the Pond. He worked as a senior producer at BBC Radio 3 until he left in 2005.

Pitts founded the vocal ensemble Tonus Peregrinus and directs it. The ensemble specialises in early and contemporary choral music, above all sacred music. Among his works are the oratorio Jerusalem-Yerushalayim, which appeared on album in 2017, and Lux Aeterna, a Kontakion of the Departed for Alexander Litvinenko. An earlier recording is the album Seven Letters from 2005. In 2016 he succeeded Roland Peelman as artistic director of The Song Company, Australia's national vocal ensemble. He is the brother of the composer and teacher John Pitts.

Pitts works on the border between early and new choral music. He shows how a contemporary composer can continue the tradition of polyphonic church singing and still say something new.
artiest/antony-pitts.listen: Listen to an excerpt of Jerusalem-Yerushalayim and notice the interplay of the voices. Try to hear where the choral sound is close and where it is open.

artiest/anuel-aa.text:
Anuel AA is the stage name of Emmanuel Gazmey Santiago, born in 1992 and raised in Carolina, Puerto Rico. He is a rapper and singer, and he and other Latin American artists call him The God of Latin trap. His father worked at the Puerto Rican branch of Sony Music, and as a child he looked up to Tupac Shakur. He started recording at fourteen and put his music online in 2010. That caught the attention of Rick Ross, who signed him to the Latin division of Maybach Music Group.

His mixtape Real Hasta la Muerte was released in February 2016 and received good reviews. In April 2016 he was arrested in Guaynabo and sentenced to thirty months in prison for illegal possession of a firearm. In prison he recorded his debut album, mainly by passing on his vocals over the telephone. That album, also called Real Hasta la Muerte, came out on 17 July 2018, the day he was released, and was a great success. Later came Emmanuel in 2020, Las leyendas nunca mueren and Los Dioses in 2021, and LLNM2 in 2022.

Latin trap mixes the heavy bass and harder rhythms of trap with Spanish-language singing and melodies from reggaeton. Anuel often uses samples and reworkings of songs that were popular in his youth. He is a controversial figure, but he gave Latin trap a face and helped bring the genre to the Billboard Hot Latin Songs charts.
artiest/anuel-aa.listen: Listen to Sola and notice the heavy bass and the sung melody that floats on top. Try to hear where the rap turns into singing.

artiest/aphex-twin.text:
Aphex Twin is the stage name of Richard D. James, a British musician, composer and DJ. He was born in Ireland in 1971 to Welsh parents and grew up in Cornwall, far from the big cities. As a child he played with the strings of the family piano and with tape recorders, and later he tinkered with electronic equipment. At twelve he bought his first synthesizer. In the late 1980s he played at illegal parties in coves and among the dunes of Cornwall, where he slipped in his own tracks on cassette.

In 1991 his first EP, Analogue Bubblebath, came out, and with a friend he founded the label Rephlex. The Belgian label R&S picked the tracks for his first album, Selected Ambient Works 85–92 (1992), from a box full of cassettes. That record, with Xtal, was largely made at home: soft, dreamy ambient techno with slow beats and warm synthesizer sounds. He then signed to Warp, and Selected Ambient Works Volume II, the Richard D. James Album (1996) and the singles Come to Daddy and Windowlicker followed, with notorious videos by Chris Cunningham.

James combines styles such as techno, ambient, acid and jungle, and his music can be soft and lovely, but also hard, fast and distorted. He is regarded as one of the most important names in so-called intelligent dance music. After Drukqs (2001) he released music for years under other names. In 2014 he returned with Syro, for which he received a Grammy. Many journalists call him one of the most influential electronic musicians of his time.
artiest/aphex-twin.listen: Listen to Xtal from 1992. Notice how the track never builds towards a climax or a drop, but keeps rolling gently along with a soft beat, warm synthesizers and a faint voice in the background.

artiest/aphrodite-s-child.text:
Aphrodite's Child was a Greek pop and rock group, formed in 1967 by Evangelos Papathanassiou, later known as Vangelis (keyboards, flutes), Demis Roussos (bass, guitar, vocals), Loukas Sideras (drums, vocals) and Silver Koulouris (guitar). Papathanassiou and Roussos had already had success in Greece with The Forminx and The Idols. When a right-wing dictatorship came to power in their country, the group moved to Paris. There it signed with Mercury Records. The name came from a song by Dick Campbell.

The second single, Rain and Tears, an adaptation of Pachelbel's Canon in D, made the group famous overnight in France and other European countries, even though it was sung in English. It sold more than a million copies. I Want to Live followed, an adaptation of Plaisir d'amour, and then the albums End of the World in 1968 and It's Five O'Clock, recorded in London in 1970. The third album, 666 from 1972, is a double album based on the biblical Book of Revelation, mainly the idea of Vangelis, with the lyricist Costas Ferris. The music was much more psychedelic and progressive than earlier work. The other members wanted to stay with pop, and the group broke up.

Vangelis would later become world-famous as a film composer, and Roussos as a solo singer. The group shows how a pop audience was swept along into progressive rock.
artiest/aphrodite-s-child.listen: Listen to Rain and Tears and notice the melody of Pachelbel's Canon underneath the singing. Can you hear how a Baroque piece turns into a pop song?

artiest/aram-khachaturian.text:
Aram Khachaturian (6 June 1903 to 1 May 1978) was a Soviet-Armenian composer and conductor. He was born in Tiflis, present-day Tbilisi, into an Armenian family and grew up among Armenian, Azerbaijani and Georgian folk music. In 1921 he moved to Moscow. Without any earlier musical training he enrolled at the Gnessin Institute, and later he studied at the Moscow Conservatory with Nikolai Myaskovsky. His first major work, the piano concerto of 1936, made his name known inside and outside the Soviet Union. Among the works that followed were a violin concerto and ballets.

Khachaturian wrote the first Armenian ballet music, symphony, concerto and film music. He followed the Russian tradition, but took broad influences into it from the folk music of Armenia, the Caucasus, the Middle East and Eastern Europe. From the late 1930s he held high posts in the Union of Soviet Composers, although in 1948 he was publicly denounced as a formalist together with Prokofiev and Shostakovich, a decision that was reversed that same year. After 1950 he taught at the Gnessin Institute and the conservatory.

In Armenia he is regarded as a national hero and as the best-known Armenian composer of the twentieth century. His rhythmic, colourful orchestral music was also used outside the concert hall and has influenced a great deal of contemporary music.
artiest/aram-khachaturian.listen: Listen to a piece by Khachaturian and notice the fiery rhythms and the Eastern-tinged melody. Try to hear where the folk music resounds in the orchestra.

artiest/arcade-fire.text:
Arcade Fire is a Canadian indie rock band from Montreal. Win Butler and Josh Deu founded the group around 2001, after meeting at secondary school. At university Régine Chassagne joined, and later Richard Reed Parry, Tim Kingsbury and Jeremy Gara came on board. Earlier, in 2002, the group had recorded an EP on Butler's family farm in Maine. In 2003 it signed a contract with the independent label Merge Records.

In 2004 Funeral appeared, the debut album, which deals with the deaths of several relatives of the band members. It received glowing reviews and appears on many lists of the best albums of the 2000s. Neon Bible followed in 2007 and The Suburbs in 2010, then Reflektor in 2013, Everything Now in 2017 and WE in 2022. All the albums from Funeral to WE received a Grammy nomination for best alternative album. The band is described as indie rock, art rock and baroque pop. The members play guitar, bass, drums, piano, violin, cello, accordion, harp and many other instruments, and constantly swap places during a performance.

Arcade Fire showed that an independent label and a group with a big, almost orchestral sound could reach the rock world in the 2000s. Influences cited include David Bowie, Talking Heads, Bruce Springsteen and Roxy Music.
artiest/arcade-fire.listen: Listen to a track from Funeral and notice the layers of piano, strings and guitar that build up the sound. Can you hear how many people are playing at once?

artiest/arcangel.text:
Arcángel is the stage name of Austin Agustín Santos, born on 23 December 1985 in New York to a Dominican family. As a baby he moved with his family to Puerto Rico, and from the age of twelve he commuted between New York and the island. His mother was a member of the merengue group Las Chicas del Can. Around 2002 he wanted to become a reggaeton artist, and in Puerto Rico he met De la Ghetto. Together they formed the duo Arcángel & De la Ghetto, which signed with Baby Records, the label of the reggaeton artist Zion.

The duo never released a studio album, only individual tracks on compilation albums, including Aparentemente, Agresivo, Sorpresa and Mi Fanática. After the split in 2007 Arcángel began a solo career and founded his own label, Flow Factory, with his mother becoming his manager. His debut album El Fenómeno came out at the end of 2008, after an earlier plan, La Maravilla, was leaked. In 2012 he signed with Pina Records, and Sentimiento, Elegancia & Maldad, which followed in 2013, reached number 1 on the American Latin albums chart. Later came Los favoritos in 2015, Ares in 2018, Historias de un capricornio in 2019 and SR. SANTOS in 2022.

Arcángel is seen as one of the most influential artists of Latin urban music and as a pioneer of Latin trap. He shows how reggaeton developed from the streets of Puerto Rico into a worldwide sound.
artiest/arcangel.listen: Listen to a track by Arcángel from El Fenómeno and notice the rhythm of the reggaeton beat, the dembow, and the way he switches between rapping and singing.

artiest/arcangelo-corelli.text:
Arcangelo Corelli was born in 1653 in Fusignano, in Romagna, then part of the Papal States. His father died five weeks before he was born. He was trained in Bologna and Rome and spent most of his career in Rome, under the protection of wealthy patrons. In 1675 he was already playing there as a violinist in the oratorios of the Florentine church. Later he led festive performances for Queen Christina of Sweden and lived in the palace of Cardinal Pietro Ottoboni, where for a long time he directed the famous Monday concerts.

His entire oeuvre consists of only six published collections, five of sonatas and one of concerti grossi. Opus 5 contains twelve sonatas for violin and basso continuo, the last of which is La Follia, a series of variations on a well-known theme. Opus 6, twelve concerti grossi, appeared in 1714, a year after his death in Rome. He was buried in the Pantheon. His work was key to the development of the sonata and the concerto, established the violin as the leading instrument and for the first time brought together modern tonality and functional harmony.

Corelli's way of playing lived on in pupils such as Francesco Geminiani and Pietro Locatelli, and his music influenced a whole generation of composers, including Vivaldi, Handel and Bach. It sounds clear, balanced and songlike, without exuberant violin fireworks. The concerto grosso sets a small group of soloists against the whole orchestra. His La Follia was later used again by composers such as Rachmaninoff, who wrote piano variations on it.
artiest/arcangelo-corelli.listen: Listen to the Allegro from Concerto grosso Op. 6 No. 8. Notice how a small group of soloists and the full string orchestra alternate and answer one another.

artiest/archie-shepp.text:
Archie Shepp, born on 24 May 1937 in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, and raised in Philadelphia, is an American saxophonist, teacher and playwright. He played banjo with his father and studied piano and saxophone. From 1955 to 1959 he studied drama at Goddard College. He then played in the band of the pianist Cecil Taylor. In 1963 his first record under his own name appeared, with the trumpeter Bill Dixon. At the end of 1964 he took part in the sessions for John Coltrane's A Love Supreme and in 1965 he recorded Ascension with him.

In 1965 he made Fire Music, on which his political awareness and his Afrocentric outlook became visible, with a recitation of an elegy for Malcolm X. The Magic of Ju-Ju from 1967 was deeply rooted in African music and used an African percussion ensemble. In 1969 he played at the Pan-African Cultural Festival in Algiers. In 1972 Attica Blues appeared, a response to the uprising at Attica prison, along with The Cry of My People. Shepp also wrote plays, including The Communist and Lady Day: A Musical Tragedy. Later he also recorded blues, ballads and spirituals, such as Goin' Home with Horace Parlan in 1977.

Shepp became a professor at the University at Buffalo and then, for thirty years, at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. He shows how the avant-garde jazz of the 1960s linked music and the struggle for civil rights.
artiest/archie-shepp.listen: Listen to the opening piece of Fire Music and notice the raw, screaming tone of his tenor saxophone. Try to hear how the horns drown one another out and come together again.

artiest/arco-iris.text:
Arco Iris was an Argentinian rock group from the late 1960s to the late 1970s, important in the history of Argentinian rock. The group began as The Crows, until the producer Ricardo Kleinman signed it on condition that it sing in Spanish. The frontman and founder was Gustavo Santaolalla, together with Ara Tokatlián and Guillermo Bodarampé. The group lived in a community with Danais Wynnycka, known as Dana, who became their spiritual guide, with yoga as a way of life. Their song Blues de Dana won the Beat Festival of Mar del Plata.

The real breakthrough came in 1972, with the hit Mañana Campestre on Tiempo de resurrección. The same year saw the double album Sudamérica o el regreso a la aurora, generally regarded as the first rock opera in Spanish, with blues, folk, jazz, rock and Latin American sounds. In 1973 Inti-Raymi followed. Agitor Lucens V from 1975 was more symphonic, with long instrumental passages and plenty of keyboards. After that Santaolalla left the group. In 1978 Arco Iris moved to California and made jazz and new age.

Arco Iris was, together with the Chilean group Los Jaivas, a pioneer in blending rock and regional folk music. Santaolalla later became an important producer of rock in Spanish and a film composer.
artiest/arco-iris.listen: Listen to Mañana Campestre and notice the acoustic guitars and the melody that recalls folk music. Can you hear how the electric guitar butts in over the top?

artiest/arctic-monkeys.text:
Arctic Monkeys are an English rock band from Sheffield, founded in 2002 by neighbours and friends Alex Turner and Matt Helders, together with Andy Nicholson. Later the guitarist Jamie Cook joined and, in 2006, the bassist Nick O'Malley. The band played its first gig on 13 June 2003 at The Grapes in Sheffield. It recorded demos that it gave away free on CD, which fans then shared with one another over the internet. In this way many people heard its music before there was a contract. In 2005 it signed with the independent label Domino.

The debut album Whatever People Say I Am, That's What I'm Not appeared in 2006 and became the fastest-selling debut album in the British charts up to that time. It won the Brit Award for British Album of the Year in 2007. Favourite Worst Nightmare followed in 2007, Humbug in 2009 and Suck It and See in 2011. The international breakthrough came with AM in 2013 and the worldwide hit Do I Wanna Know?. After that, with Tranquility Base Hotel & Casino in 2018 and The Car in 2022, they chose a softer, piano-driven sound. The band won seven Brit Awards and was the first independent band to enter at number 1 with its first five albums.

Arctic Monkeys show how, in the internet age, a band could reach a large audience without a major record company. Turner's sharp lyrics about nightlife in an English city were part of this.
artiest/arctic-monkeys.listen: Listen to Do I Wanna Know? and notice the heavy, slow guitar riff and the handclaps. Can you hear how little the song needs to build tension?

artiest/aretha-franklin.text:
Aretha Franklin was born in 1942 in Memphis and grew up in Detroit, where her father C.L. Franklin was the minister of the New Bethel Baptist Church. As a child she sang in his church, and in 1956 her first gospel record appeared. Franklin became the 'Queen of Soul'. She brought gospel, soul and pop together in a single voice, and her version of Respect became a song of the civil rights movement and of the women's movement.

In 1960 she signed with Columbia, where she made records somewhere between jazz and pop, without great success. At the end of 1966 the producer Jerry Wexler brought her to Atlantic Records. In January 1967 she recorded I Never Loved a Man (The Way I Love You) at the FAME studio in Muscle Shoals, Alabama, with her own piano playing as the foundation. A month later, in New York, came Respect, a song by Otis Redding. Franklin turned it around: now it is a woman demanding respect. Her sisters Carolyn and Erma sang the backing vocals, and Carolyn came up with the idea of spelling out the word. Respect reached number 1 in the American pop and R&B charts in 1967 and won two Grammys.

In all, Franklin won eighteen Grammys. In 1987 she became the first woman to be inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Rolling Stone twice placed her at the top of its list of the greatest singers of all time. In 2009 she sang at the inauguration of President Barack Obama. She died in Detroit in 2018; a year later she received a posthumous special citation from the Pulitzer Prize.
artiest/aretha-franklin.listen: Respect (1967): notice the moment when Franklin spells out the word letter by letter, and the backing vocals of her sisters, who keep answering her singing. Halfway through, King Curtis plays a tenor saxophone solo.

artiest/ari-babakhanov.text:
Ari Babakhanov, born in 1934, is a musician from Bukhara who plays the long-necked lutes tanbur, qashqari rubab and dutar. He comes from a Jewish family with a famous musical tradition. His grandfather Levi Babakhan, who lived from 1873 to 1926, was the legendary court singer of Alim Khan, the last emir of Bukhara. His father Moshe Babakhanov, from 1910 to 1983, was also a famous singer and accompanied himself on tanbur and doira. Unlike them, Ari became a pure instrumentalist.

He studied under the European curriculum at the conservatory in Tashkent and graduated in 1959. Under Soviet policy the traditional instruments could still be used, but mainly for European repertoire. After his successes in Tashkent he returned to Bukhara and taught at the music school for forty years. With the help of his father and other musicians he slowly found his way back to the classical music of Bukhara, the Shashmaqam. He made it his life's task to preserve this art, and wrote down a great amount of music. In 1991 he founded the Shashmaqam Ensemble at the Bukhara Philharmonic, which grew from ten to nineteen members. In 1998 the CD Shashmaqam: The Tradition of Bukhara appeared.

After the independence of Uzbekistan the Jewish community of Bukhara largely left, and Babakhanov moved to Germany with his family. He is regarded as the keeper of the Shashmaqam.
artiest/ari-babakhanov.listen: Listen to a recording of Ari Babakhanov and the Shashmaqam Ensemble and notice the long-necked lute and the voice, which together follow a single melodic line. Can you hear that there are no chords with it?

artiest/ari-up.text:
Ari Up, born Ariane Forster on 17 January 1962 in Munich, was a German singer, best known from the British punk group The Slits. Her father was a schlager singer; her mother, Nora Forster, was a friend of Jimi Hendrix and married John Lydon of the Sex Pistols in 1979. At home, in her mother's house, she came into contact with punk. Joe Strummer of The Clash taught her to play the guitar. In 1976, at the age of fourteen, she founded The Slits with the drummer Palmolive. The guitarist Viv Albertine joined later.

At the end of the 1970s The Slits toured as the support act for The Clash. Ari Up's love of reggae led the group towards a jungle-like dub style. She was the most striking member, with her wild hair and clothes. After the group broke up in 1981 she lived with her family in Indonesia and Belize and then in Kingston, Jamaica. There she made music with the New Age Steppers and as a soloist under the names Baby Ari, Madussa and Ari Up. Her first solo album Dread More Dan Dead came in 2005, followed later by Return From Planet Dub in 2009 and Rare Singles and More in 2011. She also contributed to Lee Scratch Perry's Repentance in 2008.

Ari Up died on 20 October 2010 in Los Angeles, aged 48, of breast cancer. She showed that punk could also be open to reggae and dub, and that a young woman could take the lead in doing so.
artiest/ari-up.listen: Listen to a track by The Slits and notice Ari Up's shrieking, playful singing and the dub-like bass line. Try to hear how punk and reggae meet there.

artiest/ariana-grande.text:
Ariana Grande was born in 1993 in Boca Raton, Florida. As a child she already performed in musicals such as Annie and sang with orchestras. At fifteen she appeared on Broadway in the musical 13, and after that she became known as Cat Valentine in the Nickelodeon series Victorious and Sam & Cat. Her dream was to make an R&B album, and at Republic Records she got that chance.

Her debut Yours Truly (2013) was pop and R&B with a nod to the past. On My Everything (2014) and Dangerous Woman (2016) she added electronics; hits such as Problem, Break Free, Bang Bang, Into You and Side to Side came from those albums. Personal setbacks coloured Sweetener (2018) and thank u, next (2019), which feature trap beats and hits such as thank u, next and 7 rings. Then followed Positions (2020), the danceable eternal sunshine (2024) and the electronic petal (2026). She also played Glinda in the film Wicked.

Grande is known for her four-octave vocal range, up into the high whistle register. Many of her big hits came about with Swedish hitmakers such as Max Martin, who also worked for Katy Perry and Taylor Swift. In this way she fits into the line of the modern hit factory: a strong voice, a team of experienced writers and producers, and songs built down to the smallest detail to stick in the mind.
artiest/ariana-grande.listen: Listen to Problem. Notice the short saxophone riff that keeps coming back, and the whispered line from a male voice in the chorus. Hear how Grande lets her voice climb above it.

artiest/armin-van-buuren.text:
Armin van Buuren was born in 1976 in Leiden and grew up in Koudekerk aan den Rijn. He studied law at Leiden University, put that degree on hold for music and graduated after all in 2003. Around 2000, with Tiësto and Ferry Corsten, he was one of the Dutch DJs who played trance all over the world. The British magazine DJ Mag proclaimed him the world's best DJ five times: in 2007, 2008, 2009, 2010 and 2012.

His breakthrough as a producer was Communication. He made the track entirely on his own, in two days, and it was released in July 1999 on 12-inch in the Netherlands. It is an instrumental trance track without vocals. In 2000 it reached number 18 in the British charts. At the start of 1999 he began his own label Armind, and in 2003, with Maykel Piron and David Lewis, he founded Armada Music, with its headquarters in Amsterdam. That same year his first album, 76, appeared. Since 2001 he has presented the weekly radio show A State of Trance.

With Armada he also became an entrepreneur in dance music. On 30 April 2013 he played in Amsterdam at the party around the inauguration of King Willem-Alexander. He was nominated for a Grammy for This Is What It Feels Like. Van Buuren belongs to the generation that made trance a Dutch export product, together with organisers such as ID&T and the Amsterdam Dance Event.
artiest/armin-van-buuren.listen: Communication is entirely instrumental: the melody lies with the synthesizers, not with a voice. In the long 12-inch version, of well over nine minutes, listen to how the layers come in one by one, so that as a DJ you have time to mix into the next track.

artiest/arnold-fishkin.text:
Arnold Fishkin, more often Arnold Fishkind in the sources, was an American jazz bassist, born on 20 July 1919 in Bayonne, New Jersey. He grew up in Freeport on Long Island, where he formed a lifelong friendship with Chubby Jackson. He began on the violin at the age of seven, and at fourteen he played bass. His first professional work was in 1937 with Bunny Berigan. After that he played with Jack Teagarden and Les Brown. Three years of service in the Second World War interrupted his career.

In 1946 he met the pianist Lennie Tristano in New York. From 1947 to 1949 he played with him, and afterwards he recorded with Lee Konitz and on Johnny Smith's Moonlight in Vermont. He also played with Charlie Barnet, where he met Stan Getz. In the 1950s he became a much-in-demand studio musician for radio, television and pop singers such as Frankie Laine. He worked for fifteen years at ABC and played, among other things, in The Andy Williams Show in 1961. Jack Kerouac mentioned him in his novel Visions of Cody. Later he moved to California, where he worked for the television shows of Dean Martin and Bob Hope. He also toured with Les Brown and Lena Horne. Fishkind appeared on more than a hundred albums and named Jimmy Blanton as his greatest example.

In the 1970s he converted to Christianity and became an elder in the community of Keith Green. He died in 1999 in Palm Desert. He shows how many jazz bassists worked in studios and television orchestras, out of sight of the big magazines.
artiest/arnold-fishkin.listen: Listen to a recording on which Fishkin or Fishkind plays bass and notice the bass, which carries the rhythm and the chords. Try to hear how that line supports the soloists.

artiest/arnold-schonberg.text: Arnold Schoenberg of Vienna began in the late Romantic style of Wagner and Mahler and around 1908 let go of the tonic altogether, which he called the emancipation of the dissonance. In Pierrot lunaire of 1912 the voice hovers between speaking and singing, a technique called Sprechstimme. Around 1923 he developed the twelve-tone method, in which all twelve tones in a fixed row are of equal standing. As a teacher in Vienna, Berlin and Los Angeles he shaped generations of composers.
artiest/arnold-schonberg.listen: Listen to Mondestrunken and hear how the singer half speaks and half sings the text, above a piano that keeps repeating the same glittering little figure.

artiest/art-blakey.text: The drummer Art Blakey, from Pittsburgh, played in the 1940s in Billy Eckstine's big band, where Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie also played. In 1954 he recorded A Night at Birdland with the pianist Horace Silver and the trumpeter Clifford Brown. From that collaboration grew the Jazz Messengers, whom Blakey led until his death in 1990. His playing was powerful, with a driving roll on the snare drum and a hi-hat that snaps shut on two and four. The Jazz Messengers was a school for young talent: Lee Morgan, Wayne Shorter, Freddie Hubbard, Wynton and Branford Marsalis and many others began there. Moanin' (1958), with the pianist Bobby Timmons, became the band's best-known record.
artiest/art-blakey.listen: Hear the roll of the drums pushing the soloist forward.

artiest/art-blakey-en-the-jazz-messenger.text:
The Jazz Messengers were a jazz combo that existed for more than thirty-five years, from the early 1950s until the death of the drummer Art Blakey in 1990. Blakey led the group from the start, and the names Art Blakey and Jazz Messengers became synonymous. In 1947 he had already recorded under the name Art Blakey's Messengers for Blue Note. Around 1953 and 1954 he worked with Horace Silver, and in February 1954 the live album A Night at Birdland appeared, with Clifford Brown and Lou Donaldson, among others. Some see that as the beginning of the group.

The group grew into a proving ground for young talent. New young players kept coming in, and a spell with the Messengers was regarded as a rite of passage. Many alumni became leaders in their own right, such as Lee Morgan, Benny Golson, Wayne Shorter, Freddie Hubbard, Bobby Timmons, Keith Jarrett and later Wynton and Branford Marsalis. In 1958 Blakey formed a new line-up with four musicians from Philadelphia: Lee Morgan, Benny Golson, Bobby Timmons and Jymie Merritt. That was perhaps the most fruitful period. The first record for Blue Note brought them their biggest hit, Moanin'.

The music is hard bop: warm, bluesy jazz with a solid rhythm, sturdy horn lines and plenty of room for solos. Blakey held his group to the principle that he kept the young players around, because it keeps the mind active. In this way he brought generations of jazz musicians to public attention.
artiest/art-blakey-en-the-jazz-messenger.listen: Listen to Moanin' and notice the call and response between the piano and the horns at the start. Hear how the drums drive the group on while the soloists play in turn.

artiest/art-blakey-s-jazz-messengers.text:
The Jazz Messengers were a jazz group around the drummer Art Blakey that existed for more than thirty-five years, from the early 1950s until Blakey's death in 1990. As early as 1947 Blakey recorded for Blue Note with a group called Art Blakey's Messengers. The real Jazz Messengers came into being around 1954 and 1955 in New York, as a collective of Blakey and the pianist Horace Silver, with Kenny Dorham and Hank Mobley, among others. The first records under that name were live recordings at Café Bohemia. After Silver left in 1956 Blakey kept the name.

In 1958 Blakey formed a new line-up with four musicians from Philadelphia: Lee Morgan, Benny Golson, Bobby Timmons and Jymie Merritt. Their album Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers produced the group's biggest hit: Moanin'. After that the saxophonist Wayne Shorter joined, and records such as A Night in Tunisia, Mosaic and Free for All followed. The music was hard bop: jazz with the speed of bebop, but with more blues, more gospel and a solid, swinging groove, driven on by Blakey's powerful drumming.

The most important thing about the Messengers was their role as a training ground. Blakey kept taking young musicians into his band. Anyone who had played with him counted in the jazz world. Freddie Hubbard, Keith Jarrett, Chuck Mangione and later Wynton and Branford Marsalis began their careers there. In this way the group remained, for decades, the most important school of hard bop.
artiest/art-blakey-s-jazz-messengers.listen: Listen to Moanin' by Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers. Notice the opening, where the piano plays a short phrase and the horns answer, as in a church service. Then hear how Blakey drives the soloists on with his drums.

artiest/art-ensemble-of-chicago.text:
The Art Ensemble of Chicago is an avant-garde jazz group that emerged in the late 1960s from the Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians, or AACM for short. Members of the later group played under various names in the mid-1960s, including as the Roscoe Mitchell Sextet on the 1966 album Sound. All the musicians played several instruments. Joseph Jarman and Roscoe Mitchell played alto and tenor saxophone as well as other saxophones, flute and clarinet. Lester Bowie played trumpet.

In 1968, after a farewell concert in Evanston, Illinois, the group left for Paris, where it played at the Théâtre du Vieux Colombier. There it got the name Art Ensemble of Chicago, because a French promoter added of Chicago to it. The name stuck, because the members felt it expressed their collaboration better. In 1969 A Jackson in Your House, Message to Our Folks and People in Sorrow appeared, among others, and in 1970 Certain Blacks and Go Home. Lester Bowie died in 1999, Malachi Favors in 2004 and Joseph Jarman in 2019.

The ensemble combined many jazz styles and also used small instruments such as bells, bicycle horns, party whistles and wind gongs. On stage the members wore costumes and Jarman painted his face, to represent everyone in the universe. In this way the ensemble showed that jazz did not have to stay with Western instruments.
artiest/art-ensemble-of-chicago.listen: Listen to Thème de Yoyo and notice the small instruments and percussion alongside the horns. Try to hear how silence and sound alternate.

artiest/art-garfunkel.text:
Art Garfunkel, born on 5 November 1941 in Forest Hills, Queens, is an American singer, actor and poet, best known from the folk rock duo Simon & Garfunkel. He met Paul Simon in a school production of Alice in Wonderland. Between 1956 and 1962 they performed as Tom & Jerry, modelled on the Everly Brothers, with whom they shared the close two-part harmony. Their single Hey, Schoolgirl reached number 49 in the charts in 1957. After that Garfunkel studied architecture at Columbia University.

In 1963 they re-formed the duo as Simon and Garfunkel. Their first album Wednesday Morning, 3 A.M. from 1964 flopped, but the producer Tom Wilson added electric backing to The Sound of Silence, which became number 1 in 1965. Four influential albums followed, including Bookends and Bridge over Troubled Water. For the film The Graduate in 1967 they made Mrs. Robinson. Garfunkel did not write songs himself, but he was the vocal arranger and wrote Canticle to go with Scarborough Fair. After Bridge over Troubled Water in 1970 they split up.

As a solo artist Garfunkel made albums such as Angel Clare in 1973, Breakaway in 1975 and Watermark in 1978, and he had two number ones in the United Kingdom. In 1990 the duo was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. His clear, high tenor gave Simon's songs their soft glow.
artiest/art-garfunkel.listen: Listen to The Sound of Silence and notice the two-part singing of Simon and Garfunkel. Can you hear how their voices sound almost as one?

artiest/art-of-noise.text:
Art of Noise was a British avant-garde and electronic group, formed in early 1983 by the sound engineer Gary Langan, the programmer J. J. Jeczalik, the keyboard player and arranger Anne Dudley, the producer Trevor Horn and the music journalist Paul Morley. It began during the recording of the Yes album 90125, when Jeczalik and Langan put a discarded drum riff by Alan White into the Fairlight sampler, the first time a whole drum pattern was sampled. The name comes from the essay The Art of Noises by the Futurist Luigi Russolo.

In September 1983 the EP Into Battle with the Art of Noise appeared on Horn's label ZTT, with Beat Box as a hit in the dance clubs. In 1984 the first album followed, (Who's Afraid of) The Art of Noise? The group presented itself as faceless, with masks and few performances, so that the music was at the centre. After that came In Visible Silence in 1986, In No Sense? Nonsense! in 1987 and Below the Waste in 1989. International hits were Kiss with Tom Jones and the instrumental Peter Gunn, which won a Grammy in 1986. The music mostly consisted of instrumental collages of samples, made with digital technology that was new at the time.

The group is known for its innovative use of electronics and computers in pop music. It showed that a sampler could be an instrument with which you build music from everyday sounds.
artiest/art-of-noise.listen: Listen to Beat Box and notice the chopped, stuttering sounds and the tight drum patterns. Try to hear which sounds come from a sampler.

artiest/art-pepper.text:
Art Pepper (1 September 1925 to 15 June 1982) was an American jazz musician, above all an alto saxophonist, born in Gardena, California. He had a rough childhood, with parents who were alcoholics, and grew up partly with his grandmother. He began on the clarinet at the age of nine and chose the alto saxophone at thirteen. At seventeen he played professionally with Benny Carter and then joined the orchestra of Stan Kenton. After the war he returned to Los Angeles. In the 1950s he was regarded as one of the best alto saxophonists, second only to Charlie Parker in a DownBeat readers' poll.

Pepper belonged to West Coast jazz. His records from that time include Playboys in 1956, Art Pepper Meets the Rhythm Section in 1957, Surf Ride and The Return of Art Pepper in 1957, and Art Pepper + Eleven in 1959. Because of his heroin addiction he was in prison several times, including San Quentin, but his playing remained strong. In 1968 and 1969 he played in Buddy Rich's big band. After a methadone programme in the mid-1970s he toured Europe and Japan and recorded many albums for Galaxy Records, such as Living Legend and Art Pepper Today. He wrote his autobiography Straight Life, published in 1980, with his third wife Laurie.

Pepper was known for his emotionally charged playing and for several changes of style. He died of a stroke. His work shows how intense jazz can sound when the musician puts his own struggle into every song.
artiest/art-pepper.listen: Listen to a ballad by Art Pepper, for example from Art Pepper Meets the Rhythm Section, and notice the tone of his alto saxophone. Can you hear how he makes a single note tremble with feeling?

artiest/art-tatum.text: Art Tatum, from Toledo, Ohio, was almost blind and learned to play the piano by ear; he named Fats Waller as his great example. In 1932 he moved to New York, where in 1933 he recorded his first solos, with a lightning-fast Tiger Rag. His technique was so great that fellow pianists were astonished by it. Tatum mostly played well-known songs and filled them with fast runs, unexpected modulations and reharmonisations: new chords under an existing melody. That harmonic freedom inspired the bebop musicians. From 1953 to 1955 he recorded more than a hundred solo pieces for the producer Norman Granz. He died in 1956 of kidney disease.
artiest/art-tatum.listen: Listen to how a familiar melody keeps turning up in different chords.

artiest/art-taylor.text:
Art Taylor, in full Arthur S. Taylor Jr., was an American jazz drummer, born in 1929 in New York. He grew up on Sugar Hill in Harlem and as a teenager played in a local band with Sonny Rollins, Jackie McLean and Kenny Drew. He soon worked with big names from bebop and hard bop: Howard McGhee, Coleman Hawkins, Buddy DeFranco and above all Bud Powell, for whom he often sat behind the drums in the 1950s. He also recorded with Miles Davis, Gene Ammons and John Coltrane.

In 1956 Taylor started his own group, Taylor's Wailers. The debut album Taylor's Wailers appeared in 1957 and contains swinging hard bop with Donald Byrd, Jackie McLean and Charlie Rouse, among others. It includes two pieces by Thelonious Monk: Well, You Needn't and Off Minor. Later came Taylor's Tenors in 1959 and A.T.'s Delight in 1960, among others. In 1963 he moved to Europe, where for seventeen years he lived mainly in France and Belgium and took lessons from Kenny Clarke. In 1977 he wrote Notes and Tones, a book of interviews with other musicians, in which they also spoke about the social side of their profession.

Taylor worked mainly as an accompanist and played on hundreds of recording sessions. His strength lay in listening: he adapted to the soloist instead of drowning him out. Coltrane said that he chose him because his playing did not get in his way. His sense of rhythm was influenced by Kenny Clarke, Art Blakey and Max Roach, and by the piano rhythms of Bud Powell. In his drumming you can hear how a good accompanist carries a group without drawing attention to himself.
artiest/art-taylor.listen: Listen to Well, You Needn't on Taylor's Wailers from 1957. Notice how the drums follow the soloists and push them on without drowning out the conversation between the horns.

artiest/artful-dodger.text:
Artful Dodger was a British UK garage duo, initially consisting of the songwriters and producers Mark Hill and Pete Devereux. In the 1990s and early 2000s they scored seven consecutive singles in the British top twenty. What began as an alias for underground bootlegs grew into a project with its own songs. In 2000 Hill and Devereux were named British Producers of the Year, and they received recognition from the Ivor Novello Awards for their songwriting.

Mark Hill came to the music school of the University of Southampton as a percussionist. He had played with the Welsh Philharmonic Orchestra, in jazz bands and as a session musician. In his second year he joined a jazz-funk band and, with a fellow student, Neil Kerr, started a recording studio. There the first releases on their own label, Centric Records, came into being, including Something, What Ya Gonna Do and above all Re-Rewind. The track first appeared as a white label and was then licensed to other labels. The album It's All About the Stragglers came out in 2000.

UK garage is dance music with a fast, syncopated rhythm, a bouncing bass and soulful vocals, a British successor to house and jungle. Artful Dodger showed how musically trained studio musicians could bring that sound into the charts, with catchy vocal lines and clever production.
artiest/artful-dodger.listen: Listen to Re-Rewind the Crowd Say Bo Selecta and notice the syncopated rhythm, the low bass and the repeated shout that whips up the crowd. Try to hear how the vocals form part of the beat.

artiest/arthur-baker.text:
Arthur Baker is an American producer and DJ, born in 1955 in Boston. In the 1970s he played soul and Philly soul in Boston clubs. He learned to record in a studio and, with borrowed money, made a disco album full of strings, in the style of Gamble and Huff. In 1981 he moved to New York, where as North End he had his first hit with Happy Days.

For the hip hop label Tommy Boy he produced Planet Rock by Afrika Bambaataa and the Soul Sonic Force in 1982. The track combined melodies from Kraftwerk's Trans Europe Express and Numbers. These were not sampled but replayed by studio musicians. After that Baker made dance remixes of rock and pop hits, such as Girls Just Wanna Have Fun by Cyndi Lauper and Dancing in the Dark by Bruce Springsteen. He wrote Confusion together with New Order, gave Hall & Oates a more electronic sound on Big Bam Boom and helped Bob Dylan with Empire Burlesque. In 1985 he organised, with Steven Van Zandt, the anti-apartheid song Sun City.

Baker worked at a time when remixes were still made with tape and scissors. He built bridges between hip hop, disco, electronic music and rock. Planet Rock thus became the basis of electro: cool drum machines and synthesizers from Europe, combined with the breakbeats and raps of the Bronx.
artiest/arthur-baker.listen: Listen to Planet Rock by Afrika Bambaataa and the Soul Sonic Force. Notice the hard, dry hits of the drum machine and the synthesizer melody that you may recognise from Kraftwerk. Hear how the raps go over it like a festive call.

artiest/arthur-bliss.text:
Sir Arthur Bliss was born in 1891 in Barnes, then still in Surrey, the eldest of three sons of a businessman from Massachusetts. His mother died when he was four and his father passed on to him a love of the arts. He studied classics and music at Cambridge and then spent a year at the Royal College of Music, where Ralph Vaughan Williams and Gustav Holst inspired him more than his teacher Charles Stanford. His studies were cut short by the First World War, in which he served with distinction.

After the war he was known as a headstrong, modernist composer. His works include A Colour Symphony, the cello concerto, the ballets Checkmate and Miracle in the Gorbals and the clarinet quintet. He wrote the music for the 1936 film Things to Come, including a march. In the Second World War he returned from the United States to England to work for the BBC, where he became director of music. After the war he became Master of the Queen's Music. He died in 1975.

In his later years his music was valued but also found old-fashioned, and it faded into the shadow of younger colleagues such as William Walton and Benjamin Britten. After his death many recordings have appeared, and part of his work has remained in the British repertoire. Bliss shows how a composer from the classical tradition also wrote for the cinema, with a solid, rhythmic orchestral sound.
artiest/arthur-bliss.listen: Listen to the march from Things to Come and notice the march rhythm and the brass. Try to hear how the music gathers more and more power.

artiest/arthur-blythe.text:
Arthur Blythe was an American alto saxophonist and composer, born in 1940 in Los Angeles and raised in San Diego. He began on the alto saxophone at the age of nine and as a teenager played rhythm and blues, until he discovered jazz. In the 1960s he belonged to Horace Tapscott's Underground Musicians and Artists Association, on whose 1969 album The Giant Is Awakened he made his recording debut. In the mid-1970s he moved to New York, where he played with Chico Hamilton, Gil Evans, Lester Bowie, Jack DeJohnette and McCoy Tyner.

From 1977 Blythe made his own records, first for India Navigation, then from 1978 to 1987 for Columbia. Albums such as The Grip, Bush Baby and Lenox Avenue Breakdown, from 1977 to 1979, show his personal style. Striking is the tuba of Bob Stewart, which often took the place of the double bass. Blythe also played on records by Jack DeJohnette's Special Edition, was a member of The Leaders and for a time took a seat in the World Saxophone Quartet. Later he worked for Enja and Savant. He died in 2017.

His sound is big and round, with a fast, broad vibrato and a sharp, precise sense of phrasing. Blythe stood between the avant-garde and tradition: he could play freely, but also straightforwardly, with roots in gospel and blues. Critics heard traces of Johnny Hodges and Benny Carter in his sweet tone. His unusual line-ups with tuba, guitar and African percussion made him in the 1970s one of the most individual saxophonists of his generation.
artiest/arthur-blythe.listen: Listen to Lenox Avenue Breakdown from 1979. Notice the tuba in the rhythm section and the broad vibrato of the alto saxophone.
